regions.label: Seoul & Gyeonggi
regions.intro: The capital region — where mass-market icons (Chamisul, Jangsoo) and revived royal-court spirits (Munbaeju, Hwayo) coexist. The largest catalog by sheer number, from convenience-store soju to premium Hwayo X.

regions.label: Gangwon
regions.intro: Korea's mountain province. Steep terrain and cool air give Gangwon's sools a forest-floor character — buckwheat from Bongpyeong, deodeok root from Jeongseon, pine mushroom from Yangyang, all foraged or farmed in the highlands.

regions.label: Chungcheong
regions.intro: The classic heartland of Korean rice brewing. Flat plains and abundant water made Chungcheong the birthplace of legendary yakju like Hansan Sogokju and the modern mass-market Kooksoondang line.

regions.label: Jeolla
regions.intro: Korea's culinary capital, and its sools follow suit — bold, often medicinal, richly storied. Home to Korea's only red liquor (Jindo Hongju) and the 100-day temple-aged Songhwa Baekiljoo.

regions.label: Gyeongsang
regions.intro: The deepest distilling lineage in Korea. Andong's continuous 700-year tradition since the Mongol era, Gyeongju's royal Beopju, Busan's mountain-fortress Geumjeongsanseong makgeolli — the south coast of sool history.

regions.label: Jeju
regions.intro: An island with its own brewing tradition. Volcanic water and stone-jar fermentation produce Jeju's distinctive sools — Hallasan Soju, Omegisul made with millet instead of rice, and the rare distilled Gosorisul.
